segments.text: Dhirubhai Ambani was one of India’s greatest businessmen.
His company, Reliance Industries, today earns approximately ₹2 crore every minute.
But would you believe that Dhirubhai’s journey began as an ordinary clerk?
His job involved standing in the sun for hours, filling petrol into vehicles.
This is the story of India’s most ambitious man, Dhirubhai Ambani.
The story begins in 1932.
Dhirajlal Hirachand Ambani was born in the village of Chorwad in Gujarat.
His father was a school teacher.
He was respected.
But his salary was not sufficient to run a large family.
A family of seven somehow lived in a two-room house.
But this poverty could not break Dhirubhai’s spirit.
From childhood itself, he had a different confidence and a different hunger.
People felt that this boy would definitely do something big.
At the age of 12, he came to Junagadh for his studies.
Because of his poor background,
he was admitted as a free student at Bahadur Kanji High School.
In 1940, India was still under British rule.
Therefore, in 1946, at just 14 years of age, Dhirubhai, along with his friend Krishnakant Vakharia,
formed a student organisation called Junagadh Vidyarthi Sangh.
He actively participated in the independence movement.
In 1949, he passed the matriculation examination.
But what next?
There was no money, no family business, and no connections.
At this point, an old tradition of his community showed him a path.
For decades, young Gujarati boys had been travelling to Arabian countries.
They would work for 8 to 10 years, save money,
and then return to start their own businesses.
So, at the age of 16,
Dhirubhai boarded a steamer and set out for Aden, 2,400 kilometres away from home.
In Aden, he appeared for a job interview at A. Besse & Company.
This company controlled nearly 80 percent of trade in the Red Sea region.
Its business included products such as cars, animal hides, and petroleum products.
Luckily, his interviewer was also a Gujarati — Manganbhai Patel.
In the interview, he was asked to read an article from The Times of India
and write a summary in English.
He passed this test comfortably and was given a job on the spot.
Initially, his work involved standing in the sun for hours, filling petrol into vehicles.
Along with this, he travelled from place to place marketing Shell’s petroleum, oil, and grease products.
Many years later, interviewer Mangalbhai Patel recalled that
his first impression of Dhirubhai was the way he walked.
His footsteps were heavy.
He walked as if he had somewhere to reach and very little time.
In the early 1950s, Dhirubhai noticed something interesting.
The currency used in Aden was called the Yemeni Rial.
The silver content in the Rial currency
was worth more than the exchange value of the coin itself.
Suppose the value of one riyal coin was equal to 10 British pounds.
But the market value of the silver contained in that same riyal was 12 British pounds.
This meant that you could buy one riyal coin for 10 pounds,
melt it, and sell the silver for 12 pounds.
A direct profit of 2 pounds.
Dhirubhai did exactly this.
He placed orders for as many riyals as possible with money changers.
Then he melted the coins, extracted the silver,
and sold the silver ingots to bullion dealers in London.
This operation continued for nearly three months.
But when riyals began disappearing from circulation,
the authorities grew suspicious, and Dhirubhai had to stop.
By then, however, he had already earned several lakhs.
By 1956, after multiple promotions,
Dhirubhai had become the manager of refuelling operations at the Aden military base.
But he did not limit himself only to his job.
After work, he would roam the Aden souks, observe traders, and learn from them.
Soon, he himself began trading in rice, sugar, and other commodities.
In 1954, at the age of 22, he married Kokilaben, the daughter of a postman from Jamnagar.
After marriage, she also moved to Aden with Dhirubhai.
In 1957, their first son, Mukesh Ambani, was born in Aden itself.
By 1958, Dhirubhai had spent nearly ten years in Aden.
At that point, the 26-year-old Dhirubhai decided that
the time had come to stop working for others.
It was now time to build his own empire.
With this thought, he returned to India.
In Bombay, he started a business in partnership with his cousin Champaklal Damani.
The office consisted of a 350-square-foot room, one telephone, one table, and three chairs.
The company was named Reliance Commercial Corporation.
Initially, they exported spices to Aden and textiles to Ethiopia, Somalia, and Kenya.
But very soon, Dhirubhai spotted a better business opportunity.
He observed that there was a massive demand in India for synthetic threads
such as nylon, viscose, and polyester.
The textile industry wanted to use these threads
because fabrics made from them were affordable, crease-proof, and quick-drying.
The problem was that domestic production of the thread fulfilled
only 10 to 20 percent of demand.
On the other hand, the government had imposed strict restrictions on imports,
leading to severe shortages in India.
The government had introduced a system called REP, or Replenishment Licenses.
These licenses were given to textile exporters.
For example, if exporters exported textiles worth ₹100,
they were permitted to import artificial threads worth ₹20.
The government’s idea was to balance exports and imports through this mechanism.
Dhirubhai noticed that many exporters possessed these licenses but did not use them.
So he began buying these licenses from exporters by offering them the best possible prices.
In fact, by acquiring most of the licenses, he began controlling India’s synthetic thread imports.
Due to huge demand, he sold them to Indian textile manufacturers at high profit margins.
The business was growing rapidly.
However, something was not right in the partnership between Dhirubhai and Champaklal.
Dhirubhai was an aggressive risk-taker, whereas Champaklal preferred to play safe.
The tipping point came in 1965.
Dhirubhai predicted that synthetic thread prices would rise in the future.
So he built up a huge inventory to sell later at higher prices.
Champaklal panicked and forced Dhirubhai to reduce the inventory.
Dhirubhai sold the threads, but not to someone else.
He sold them to himself.
Within two to three weeks, prices rose, and he made massive profits.
He offered Champaklal a share of the profits.
But he also told him not to interfere in a business he did not understand.
Finally, that same year, they decided to split the partnership.
Dhirubhai and his brother bought Champaklal’s shares in Reliance for ₹6 lakh.
One major reason behind Dhirubhai’s success was his futuristic thinking.
On the other hand, unsuccessful businessmen fail to evolve with time.
Even today, millions of business owners in India use physical ledger books for accounting.
Others use outdated software with complex user interfaces that require manual data entry.
But the Odoo accounting app has revolutionised accounting.
With just two clicks, a professional invoice can be created.
Sending the invoice to the customer, tracking payments,
and sending automatic reminders for late payments are all built in.
When a supplier’s bill arrives, you simply take a photo.
Odoo’s AI extracts the vendor name, date, amount, and line items.
Once you validate it, the details are automatically entered into the accounts.
Similarly, there is no longer any need to download bank statements every month
and reconcile them manually.
You simply connect Odoo to your bank.
The app automatically imports your statements.
Its smart matching engine reconciles 95 percent of transactions
with bills and invoices automatically.
Its clean dashboards display receivables, payables, and profit margins at a glance.
For detailed analysis, P&L statements, balance sheets,
and cash flow statements are generated with one click.
Your data is backed up to the cloud at regular intervals.
This allows your CA, accountant, and team to collaborate simultaneously from anywhere on any device.
Finally, the app comes pre-configured for Indian accounting standards.
It already understands GST rates, cess, HSN codes, and TDS calculations.

Within the next year, Dhirubhai chose his next destination.
He was no longer satisfied with being just a thread supplier.
Now it was time to become a textile manufacturer himself by using those threads.
He purchased land in Naroda, Gujarat.
A simple factory building was constructed.
Operations began with just four knitting machines.
Around this time, due to political instability in Aden, many Gujaratis returned to India.
As a result, Dhirubhai found ready-made managers, accountants, and salesmen for his business.
Dhirubhai noticed that there were no established brands in the Indian textile market.
Whichever product was cheaper sold more.
So he took the brilliant decision to launch his own textile brand.
That brand was Vimal.
He positioned it as a premium fabric for the mass market.
Its tagline was “Only Vimal,” which positioned it as exclusive and superior.
He spent ₹1 crore annually on advertising.
This included fashion shows, billboards, and newspapers.
For distribution, he developed a franchise-like business model
that was previously popular only in Western countries.
Around 400 shops across the country were given Vimal franchises.
As a result, by 1979, the Naroda factory had expanded to 25 lakh square feet.
The workforce had grown to 5,000 employees.
With revenues of ₹155 crore, Reliance became India’s largest textile producer.
During this time, in 1977, Dhirubhai made a decision that changed Indian stock markets forever.
He launched Reliance’s IPO.
Before this, IPOs were invested in only by business houses,
institutional investors, and wealthy families.
Reliance, however, focused on making India’s middle class its partners.
They offered 28 lakh shares at a price of ₹10 each.
The IPO was oversubscribed seven times.
In 1978, Reliance shares began trading on the Bombay and Ahmedabad stock exchanges.
Not only did the shares list at a premium, but within a few months, prices rose to ₹50.
Investors’ money was multiplied five times.
For the first time, India’s general public created such large wealth through the stock market.
But very soon, a villain entered the story.
In 1982, allegedly, a Kolkata-based bear cartel set its sights on Reliance shares.
On March 18, the cartel launched a full-scale attack on the stock.
They began short-selling Reliance shares.
Their plan was to borrow shares from the market.
They would sell them at the current price of ₹131.
As prices fell, panic selling would push prices further down.
After a week, they would buy the shares at the lower price and return them to the lenders.
The difference between the selling price and the buying price would be their profit.
This is generally how short-selling works.
Within half an hour, the bear cartel sold around 3.5 lakh Reliance shares.
The price fell from ₹131 to ₹121.
Then something unbelievable happened.
A mysterious group of buyers from West Asian countries became active.
They began buying the shares sold by the bears.
No matter how much the bears sold, these buyers absorbed the supply.
This war continued for weeks.
The bears kept selling to crash the stock.
The buyers kept purchasing, preventing demand from falling.
By April 30, instead of crashing, Reliance shares rose to ₹201.
Now the bears had to buy real shares from the market to return what they had borrowed.
They suffered massive losses on every share.
Many cartel members were completely ruined.
The real twist was that the alleged NRI buyers who purchased ₹10 crore worth of Reliance shares
were backed by none other than Dhirubhai Ambani himself.
However, no official link between the two has ever been established.
This victory made Reliance the most popular stock in the Indian market.
Dhirubhai came to be known as the messiah of small investors.
Whether in stock markets or business, Dhirubhai was winning everywhere.
But this success was not driven only by business acumen and strategy.
The 1970s and 1980s were the era of the License Raj in India.
Dhirubhai knew that to achieve anything big,
he needed strong relationships with those in power.
So whether it was the ruling party or the opposition,
he tried to maintain good relations with everyone.
Allegedly, using this influence, he got the High Unit Value Scheme approved in 1971.
Before this scheme, exporting nylon textiles allowed imports of only nylon threads.
Now, by exporting nylon, more valuable polyester filament yarn could be imported.
Reliance benefited immensely from this scheme.
There is no doubt that Dhirubhai was a genius businessman.
But when required, he knew how to use every method — persuasion, money, pressure, and strategy.
This side of him was visible in his rivalry with Nusli Wadia.
Nusli Wadia was the promoter of Bombay Dyeing.
Bombay Dyeing was a direct competitor of Reliance in textiles.
Allegedly, Dhirubhai used every weapon against Wadia.
When Bombay Dyeing was setting up a manufacturing plant,
the government mysteriously blocked its license for two years.
When plant equipment arrived,
customs detained it for four weeks under the pretext of inspection.
At the same time, a negative media campaign was launched against Wadia.
The plant was labelled junk.
It was claimed that inferior products were being manufactured there.
Many journalists who wrote these reports came to be known as the “Dirty Dozen.”
They were allegedly paid to write against Wadia.
But the business war was not one-sided.
Ramnath Goenka, owner of The Indian Express, was close to Nusli Wadia.
When Goenka felt that Dhirubhai had manipulated the media,
he deployed his entire media empire against Reliance.
He hired investigative journalist Swaminathan Gurumurthy.
He wrote several exposés against Reliance’s business practices.
By 1985, Reliance had received excise evasion notices worth around ₹27 crore.
A CBI inquiry was also initiated.
This prolonged business war took a toll on Dhirubhai.
In 1986, he suffered a massive stroke.
His family admitted him to a hospital in the United States.
For weeks, he fought between life and death.
Many believed this was the end of the Dhirubhai era.
But when he returned to India in March 1986, everyone was shocked.
The right side of his body was paralysed.
His hand was twisted.
Walking was difficult.
But the fire in his eyes remained unchanged.
The stroke may have slowed his body, but his mind was still sharp.
He immediately immersed himself in business.
He now had to fulfil the biggest dream of his life.
A dream that would transform India’s petroleum industry forever.
Until 1980, Reliance had to buy polyester threads from others to make Vimal textiles.
These threads are made from chemicals.
These chemicals come from petroleum products.
Petroleum products come from crude oil.
Crude oil is refined in refineries.
Dhirubhai wanted Reliance to control everything from crude oil refining to textile production.
This meant complete backward integration.
Work on this dream had actually begun in 1982.
Reliance built its first polyester plant at Patalganga.
The plant was expected to take at least 26 months to complete.
Under the 24-year-long leadership of Mukesh Ambani, it became operational in just 18 months.
Reliance now produced polyester threads in-house.
But it still depended on others for chemicals.
So between 1984 and 1989, plants were set up to produce PTA, MEG, and other petrochemicals.
Reliance now produced textiles, polyester, and the petrochemicals required for polyester.
But the ultimate goal still remained.
That goal was an oil refinery.
Before work on the refinery could begin, a massive twist occurred.
Due to a cloudburst during the monsoon, the Patalganga valley was hit by devastating floods.
Within hours, Reliance’s factory and machinery worth hundreds of crores were submerged.
It felt as though Dhirubhai’s dream had been pushed back by years.
Then Mukesh Ambani took charge.
As soon as the water receded, an army of workers began working at war footing.
Each machine was dismantled, cleaned, and reassembled.
Within one month, the entire plant was operational again.
Four years after the flood, in 1993, Dhirubhai finally announced his dream project.
India’s first private-sector oil refinery.
With an annual capacity of 27 million tonnes,
it was to become one of Asia’s largest refineries.
It would alone refine 25 percent of India’s crude oil.
The project cost around $6 billion.
At the time, it was India’s largest private industrial investment.
Construction began in Jamnagar in 1995.
The entire complex was completed in just three years.
Operations started in 2000.
By 2001, the refinery was operating at 107 percent capacity.
It produced fuels such as diesel, petrol, and kerosene.
It also produced petrochemicals like paraxylene and naphtha.
Around 70 to 75 percent of output was sold to external customers.
The rest was consumed internally by Reliance.
Dhirubhai’s dream of backward integration was now complete.
The refinery was built in a desert region.
So Dhirubhai planted around 66,000 mango trees nearby.
Later, another 36,800 trees were added.
This broke Mughal Emperor Akbar’s record of planting 100,000 mango trees.
In April 2002, while addressing Reliance shareholders, Dhirubhai said
that in his youth, he had worked as a salesman for a multinational energy company in Aden.
He had then dreamed of returning to India to build a global energy company for the country.
That dream had now been fulfilled.
No one knew that this would be Dhirubhai Ambani’s last shareholder address.
Two months later, on June 24, 2002, he suffered another stroke.
On July 6, 2002, he breathed his last.
Dhirubhai used to say that our dreams must be bigger.
Our ambitions higher. Our commitment deeper. And our efforts greater.
With this mindset, the son of a village schoolteacher built India’s largest company.
This was the story of Dhirubhai Ambani.
